package_info.package_manager: Windows DLL (manual deployment, not a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: Unknown (malicious variant used in this campaign)
package_info.why_malicious: The DLL is used for Phantom DLL Hijacking, allowing APT41 to execute arbitrary code under the context of a legitimate process, maintain persistence, and evade detection. It is not a legitimate version of the DLL, but a trojanized or maliciously crafted one deployed by the attacker.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when the hijacked process loads the DLL)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the DLL is loaded by a legitimate process (via DLL hijacking), establishes a connection to a hardcoded C2 domain, profiles the infected system, and exfiltrates data to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: DLLs loaded from unexpected locations that initiate network connections and exfiltrate data are highly suspicious, especially when masquerading as legitimate system components.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate DLL should only provide expected functionality to the host process and should not initiate outbound network connections or collect system information.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate DLLs may collect system info for telemetry, but only with user consent and never from a hijacked context.
key_indicators: Exported functions not matching legitimate DLL

execution_context.file_location: Executed via wmic.exe command line or script

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the attacker abuses WMIC.exe to execute a PowerShell command that downloads and executes a remote payload, enabling further code execution and persistence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: WMIC is a legitimate administration tool, but its use to launch PowerShell and download remote scripts is a common attacker technique for fileless malware and lateral movement.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal WMIC usage is for system management, not for launching PowerShell to fetch and execute remote code.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: IT automation may use WMIC for legitimate remote management, but not to download and execute code from untrusted sources.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (DCSync attack via domain controller access)
execution_context.file_location: Executed from compromised host with domain admin privileges

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the attacker uses Mimikatz to perform a DCSync attack, requesting password hashes for privileged accounts from the domain controller, enabling credential theft and lateral movement.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: DCSync requests for admin/service accounts are highly abnormal and almost always indicate malicious activity.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate users and services do not request password hashes for other accounts from the domain controller.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, red team or incident response may use DCSync for forensics, but never in normal operations.

attack_chain.action: Initial access via spear-phishing or unknown vector
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of malicious code on target system

attack_chain.action: Persistence and code execution via Phantom DLL Hijacking (malicious TSVIPSrv.dll)
attack_chain.leads_to: Establish C2 communication and system profiling

attack_chain.action: Abuse of WMIC.exe to execute PowerShell and download further payloads
attack_chain.leads_to: Deployment of additional malware and lateral movement

attack_chain.action: Credential theft via DCSync attack using Mimikatz
attack_chain.leads_to: Privilege escalation and access to admin/service accounts

attack_chain.action: Data exfiltration, financial theft, and operational disruption
attack_chain.leads_to: Final goal: data theft, financial gain, and persistent access

behavioral_signatures: DLL loaded from non-standard directory initiating outbound network connections
WMIC.exe launching PowerShell to download and execute remote scripts
Unusual system profiling and C2 beaconing from DLLs
file_indicators: Presence of Mimikatz or similar credential dumping tools
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS to suspicious or untrusted domains
LDAP replication traffic from non-DC hosts
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for DLLs loaded from non-standard directories, especially those initiating network connections. Alert on WMIC.exe processes spawning PowerShell, particularly with commands that download remote scripts. Detect DCSync attacks by monitoring for lsadump::dcsync or abnormal LDAP replication requests from non-domain controllers. Track outbound connections to known C2 domains such as time.qnapntp.com. Correlate these behaviors for early detection of APT41-style attacks.
